title: A Tiny New Tiger Cat Joins the Feline Family Tree
summary:
Attention, cat lovers: scientists have just added a brand-new branch to the feline family tree. Meet Leopardus tilcayo, a pint-size tiger cat from Bolivia — and the first new living cat species described in more than a century.

These tiny cats have slender bodies, spotted fur and ringed tails. They weigh only about two kilograms (4.4 pounds), about as much as a four-month-old domestic kitten. They appear native to the Yungas forests of the central Andes Mountains.

Scientists named and described L. tilcayo in a paper in the October 5 issue of Current Biology. The last new living cat species described by scientists was the Uruguayan pampas cat, first described in 1923.

The discovery was a surprise. Jonas Lescroart, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Antwerp in Belgium, and his team set out to narrow down how many tiger-cat species there are. They analyzed the genetics of 38 species in the Leopardus genus. They expected to find between two and possibly four distinct tiger-cat species. Instead, their analyses point to five — and one of them had never been described before.

The evidence comes from two specimens. One is a female that was treated briefly for injuries at a sanctuary in Bolivia and later released back into the wild. The second, a male named Tigrino, still lives at the sanctuary. Cat conservationist Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz met Tigrino there and noticed he looked a bit different. Curious, she genetically tested him and shared her data with Lescroart's team.

Scientists still don't yet know how many of these tiny cats exist in the wild. Lescroart says he doesn't know if we'll have to wait another 100 years for a new species. 'I did not at all expect attention at this scale,' he says.
why_it_matters: Discovering a new species shows that wild places still hold surprises, and knowing a species exists is the first step toward protecting it and its forest home.

background_read: A species is a group of animals that share the same features and can have young together, and scientists give each species a two-part Latin name.
Tiger cats are small wild cats with spotted coats that live in the Americas.
Scientists tell species apart by comparing how animals look and by studying their genes, the instructions inside cells that shape how a living thing grows.
When a wild animal is hurt or needs care, it may be looked after at a sanctuary, a safe place where animals are protected and can sometimes return to the wild.
